q: No reptile in the zoo has fur. The zoo's python is a reptile. Which statement must be true?
o: The python is the only reptile in the zoo
Every animal without fur in the zoo is a reptile
Some mammals in the zoo are reptiles
The zoo's python has no fur
x: The python belongs to the group 'reptiles in the zoo', and no member of that group has fur. The statements say nothing about which other animals lack fur.

q: The claim "All the mangoes in this crate are ripe" has been shown to be false. Which statement must be true?
o: No mango in this crate is ripe
At least one mango in this crate is not ripe
Most of the mangoes in this crate are unripe
Exactly one mango in this crate is unripe
x: To make 'all are ripe' false, only one unripe mango is needed. It does not follow that none, most or exactly one are unripe.

q: Ali will get the scholarship only if he scores above 90%. Ali got the scholarship. Which statement must be true?
o: Everyone who scored above 90% got the scholarship
Ali was the only student to get the scholarship
Ali scored above 90%
Ali scored exactly 90%
x: 'Only if' makes scoring above 90% a necessary condition, so anyone who got the scholarship must have met it. It does not say that every high scorer gets one.

q: Buses will not run on the new road unless it is repaired. Buses are now running on the road. Which statement must be true?
o: The road was never damaged
The road has been repaired
Buses run on every repaired road
Cars are not allowed on the road
x: 'Not B unless A' means that if the road is not repaired, buses do not run. Since buses are running, the road must have been repaired.

q: Which statement means exactly the same as "If a number is divisible by 6, it is divisible by 3"?
o: If a number is divisible by 3, it is divisible by 6
If a number is not divisible by 6, it is not divisible by 3
If a number is not divisible by 3, it is not divisible by 6
Some numbers divisible by 6 are not divisible by 3
x: The contrapositive (if not 3, then not 6) always has the same meaning as the original. Reversing it fails: 9 is divisible by 3 but not by 6.

q: Every member of group P also belongs to group Q. A few members of group R do not belong to group Q. What can be concluded for certain?
o: Some members of P are not in R
No member of R is in P
Some members of Q are not in P
Some members of R are not in P
x: Every P is a Q, so anything outside Q cannot be in P. The members of R that are outside Q are therefore outside P.

q: Four books P, Q, R and S stand in a row. S is to the left of P, P is to the left of Q, and R is to the right of Q. Which statement must be true?
o: P is at the right end
R is second from the left
S is next to Q
Q is third from the left
x: The only order that fits is S, P, Q, R from the left, so Q is third. P is second, R is at the right end and S is not next to Q.

q: Ali, Bilal and Hamza scored different marks in a test. Ali did not score the highest. Hamza did not score the lowest. Bilal scored more than Hamza. Which statement must be true?
o: Hamza scored the highest marks
Bilal scored the lowest marks
Ali scored the lowest marks
Ali scored more than Hamza
x: Bilal beat Hamza, so Hamza is not highest; Hamza is not lowest either, so he is in the middle. Ali is not highest, so Ali is lowest and Bilal highest.

q: Which pair of numbers shows that the claim "The sum of any two prime numbers is even" is false?
o: 3 and 5
2 and 3
5 and 7
11 and 13
x: 2 + 3 = 5, which is odd, so this one pair disproves the claim. The other pairs are both odd primes, and their sums are even.

q: A college rule says: "A student who is absent for more than 10 days will not be allowed to sit the exam." Sana was absent for 7 days. Which statement is correct?
o: Sana will certainly be allowed to sit the exam
The rule alone does not tell us whether Sana may sit the exam
Sana will not be allowed to sit the exam
Sana has broken the college rule
x: The rule only says what happens after more than 10 days of absence. It says nothing about students absent for fewer days, so other rules could still apply to Sana.

q: A doctor claims: "Every patient who took the new tablet recovered." Which observation would prove the claim false?
o: A patient who did not take the tablet recovered
A patient who took the new tablet did not recover
Some patients refused to take the tablet
The tablet was more costly than other tablets
x: An 'every' claim is disproved by one case where the condition holds but the result does not. Patients who did not take the tablet are outside the claim.

q: Three different whole numbers, each greater than 1, add up to 10. Which statement must be true?
o: One of the numbers is 4
All three numbers are odd
One of the numbers is 6
One of the numbers is 5
x: The only set of three different whole numbers above 1 with a sum of 10 is 2, 3 and 5. So one number must be 5; none is 4 or 6, and 2 is even.

q: Statement: Should smoking be banned inside hospitals? Argument I: Yes, smoke harms patients who are already ill. Argument II: No, smokers like to smoke wherever they want. Which argument is strong?
o: Only argument II is strong
Both arguments I and II are strong
Only argument I is strong
Neither argument I nor II is strong
x: Argument I gives a real, important reason linked to patients' health. Argument II rests only on smokers' wishes, which is not a strong reason.

q: Statement: Should every college have a staff member trained in first aid? Argument I: Yes, injuries and fainting can happen at any time, and quick first aid can prevent harm. Argument II: No, every city already has a hospital. Which argument is strong?
o: Only argument II is strong
Both arguments I and II are strong
Only argument I is strong
Neither argument I nor II is strong
x: Argument I gives a practical reason about help in the first minutes. Argument II is weak because a hospital may be far away when help is needed at once.

q: Statement: Should the medical entry test be held twice a year? Argument I: Yes, a student who is ill on the test day would get another chance within the same year. Argument II: No, students would get bored of preparing for the same test. Which argument is strong?
o: Only argument I is strong
Both arguments I and II are strong
Only argument II is strong
Neither argument I nor II is strong
x: Argument I gives a real, important benefit directly linked to the proposal. Argument II rests on a trivial, personal feeling rather than a serious consequence, so it is weak.

q: Statement: Should candidates be allowed to bring calculators into the entry test? Argument I: Yes, all students like using calculators. Argument II: No, calculators are made in other countries. Which argument is strong?
o: Neither argument I nor II is strong
Only argument I is strong
Only argument II is strong
Both arguments I and II are strong
x: Liking something is not a reason to allow it, and where a calculator is made has nothing to do with fair testing. Neither argument is strong.

q: Hamza's mother tells him: "Take an umbrella; the weather report says it will rain this afternoon." Which assumption is she making?
o: It rains every afternoon
Hamza does not own an umbrella
Umbrellas are cheap to buy
The weather report is reasonably reliable
x: Her advice only makes sense if she trusts the forecast. She does not suggest it always rains, and she assumes Hamza can take an umbrella, not that he lacks one.

q: A sign in a hospital ward says: "Please keep your voices low; patients are resting." Which assumption does the sign make?
o: Visitors never talk in hospitals
All patients in the ward are asleep
Patients cannot hear normal speech
Loud voices can disturb resting patients
x: Asking for quiet so that patients can rest assumes noise could disturb them. It does not claim every patient is asleep.

q: A city's transport department says: "Our new buses will run every 10 minutes so that people leave their cars at home." Which assumption does the department make?
o: Nobody in the city owns a car
Some car users would switch to a frequent bus service
Buses are faster than cars on every road
All buses in the city are new
x: The plan only works if a frequent service would attract at least some car users. It does not need to assume buses beat cars on every road.

q: Which evidence gives the strongest support for the belief that seat belts reduce injuries in car crashes?
o: Most new cars are sold with seat belts already fitted
A well-known driver always wears his seat belt
Many people find seat belts uncomfortable on long journeys
In crashes at similar speeds, belted passengers had fewer serious injuries than unbelted ones
x: Comparing belted and unbelted people in similar crashes tests the belief directly. That cars have belts, or a famous person uses one, says nothing about injuries.

q: A coin is suspected of being unfair. Which result gives the best reason to believe that it is fair?
o: In 1000 tosses it landed heads 497 times
In 4 tosses it landed heads 3 times
It looks the same on both sides
The shopkeeper said it was a normal coin
x: A large number of tosses landing heads close to half the time is real evidence of fairness. Four tosses are far too few, and looks or someone's word are not tests.

q: Argument: "Our town's air is cleaner this year because the brick kilns switched to cleaner technology." Which fact, if true, most strengthens this argument?
o: The town had much more rain than usual this year
The new kiln technology was expensive to install
Nearby towns whose kilns did not switch showed no improvement in their air
Many people in the town bought new cars this year
x: If similar towns without the change did not improve, the kilns become the likely reason. Extra rain would offer another explanation and so weaken the argument.

q: Which reason gives a sound basis for believing that a news report is true?
o: It has been shared by many people on social media
It is written in an exciting and dramatic style
It agrees with what the reader already believed
It is confirmed by several independent and reliable sources
x: Independent, reliable confirmation is evidence. Popularity, style and agreement with our own views do not show that a report is true.

q: Saad says: "If we allow students one late submission, soon nobody will submit anything on time and the college will collapse." Which error in reasoning is this?
o: Hasty generalisation
Personal attack
Slippery slope
Circular reasoning
x: Saad claims that one small step will lead to a chain of extreme results without showing why each step must follow. That is a slippery slope.

q: A fair coin has landed heads five times in a row. Fatima believes the next toss is more likely to be tails. Why is her belief false?
o: Each toss is independent, so the chance of tails is still one half
After five heads, heads becomes more likely
A coin cannot land heads five times in a row
Tails becomes certain after five heads
x: A fair coin has no memory: earlier tosses do not change the next result. The chance stays one half for heads and one half for tails.

q: "Our family has always put toothpaste on burns, so it must be the right treatment." What is wrong with this reasoning?
o: It attacks the person instead of the argument
It treats a practice as correct only because it has been done for a long time
It draws a rule from too few cases
It confuses cause and effect
x: A long tradition is not evidence that a treatment works. Whether a remedy is right must be judged by evidence, not by how long it has been used.

q: Sara says students need more sleep before exams. Hamza replies, "So Sara wants us to sleep all day and never study!" What is wrong with Hamza's reply?
o: He twists her claim into an extreme one and argues against that instead
He agrees with Sara but uses different words
He gives scientific evidence against her claim
He draws a general rule from one example
x: Sara asked for more sleep, not sleeping all day. Hamza attacks a distorted version of her point, so he never answers what she actually said.

q: "Every player in the team is excellent, so the team must be excellent." Why is this belief not necessarily true?
o: What is true of each part is not always true of the whole
Excellent players never play in teams
A team cannot be judged at all
The claim attacks the players personally
x: A team also depends on teamwork and planning, so excellent individuals do not guarantee an excellent team. Reasoning from parts to the whole can fail.

q: Records show that elderly people who use walking sticks fall more often than those who do not. Someone concludes that walking sticks cause falls. What is the main flaw?
o: People who are already unsteady on their feet are the ones more likely to use sticks
Walking sticks are made of wood, which is slippery
Elderly people never fall without a reason
Only a few elderly people use walking sticks
x: The link may run the other way: poor balance leads people to use sticks, and poor balance also causes falls. The stick need not be the cause.

q: An advertisement shows ten students who used a certain guidebook and got into medical college. What is the main flaw in using this as proof that the book works?
o: It names too many students
Medical colleges do not allow guidebooks
It shows only the successful users and ignores those who did not get in
The students may have bought the book from different shops
x: Picking only the successes hides how many users failed. Without the full picture, ten success stories prove nothing about the book.

q: A doctor advises a patient to stop smoking. The patient replies, "You smoke too, so your advice is wrong." Why is the patient's reply a false argument?
o: Doctors are not allowed to smoke
Whether the doctor smokes does not change whether the advice is correct
The patient has not smoked for very long
The doctor did not give any advice
x: The advice is right or wrong on the evidence about smoking. Pointing out that the adviser does the same thing does not answer the advice.

q: Kamran believes that antibiotics will cure his common cold because antibiotics kill bacteria. Why is his belief false?
o: The common cold is caused by viruses, which antibiotics do not kill
Antibiotics kill only fungi
The common cold is caused by bacteria that resist all medicines
Antibiotics work only on children
x: Antibiotics act against bacteria, but a common cold is a viral infection. His reasoning starts from a true fact and applies it to the wrong kind of germ.

q: In a town, 80% of road accidents involve cars driven by men. Someone concludes that men are worse drivers than women. Which missing fact is most needed before this conclusion can be judged?
o: What share of the cars on the town's roads are driven by men
How many hospitals there are in the town
The average price of a car in the town
How many accidents happened in the previous year
x: If men drive about 80% of the cars, 80% of accidents is exactly what we would expect. Without the share of drivers, the figure says nothing about skill.

q: Which belief is based on evidence rather than being a false belief?
o: Washing hands with soap reduces the spread of germs
A black cat crossing your path brings bad luck
Wearing a lucky ring raises exam marks
Breaking a mirror causes years of misfortune
x: Handwashing with soap removing germs is shown by experiments and observation. The other three have no known cause-and-effect link and are superstitions.
